Federated Self-Supervised Modulation Classification under Non-IID and Imbalanced Data

Usman Akram, Yiyue Chen, and Haris Vikalo Affiliation:  Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA
usman.akram@austin.utexas.edu, yiyuechen@utexas.edu, hvikalo@ece.utexas.edu
Abstract

Automatic modulation classification (AMC) is a core enabler of cognitive wireless systems, providing spectrum awareness and supporting adaptive communication at the network edge. However, training AMC models on centrally aggregated data incurs high communication overhead, raises privacy concerns, and often lacks robustness to real-world conditions. We propose FedSSL-AMC, a federated self-supervised framework for learning AMC models from sparsely labeled, distributed I/Q time-series data. Participating clients collaboratively train a causal, time-dilated CNN encoder using triplet-loss self-supervision on unlabeled signals, followed by lightweight local SVMs trained on limited labeled samples. This enables communication-round-efficient, robust representation learning under class imbalance and channel variability. We establish convergence guarantees for a proximal variant of the encoder-training procedure and derive a separability bound for the downstream classifier under feature noise. Experiments on synthetic and over-the-air datasets demonstrate improvements over supervised FL baselines across all three datasets and nearly all evaluated settings involving heterogeneous SNRs, carrier-frequency offsets, and non-IID label distributions.

Index Terms: 
Federated self-supervised learning; Distributed learning; Automatic modulation classification; Data heterogeneity.

I Introduction

Next-generation wireless networks must support high-density connectivity and dynamic spectrum access as IoT growth increases demand on limited spectrum resources. Achieving this goal requires spectrum intelligence, i.e., real-time awareness of channel conditions and signal types to enable interference mitigation, adaptive modulation, and opportunistic spectrum access. Automatic modulation classification (AMC), an essential tool for acquiring spectral awareness, has received considerable attention in recent years, with numerous deep-learning approaches proposed [19, 31, 12, 36, 35, 27, 13, 34, 14]. However, most of these methods rely on centralized training, which incurs substantial bandwidth costs, raises privacy concerns, and often yields models that lack robustness to channel mismatch. Federated learning (FL) offers an alternative by enabling distributed training across edge clients without requiring raw I/Q samples to be shared [21, 30, 40]. However, the performance of standard FL methods can degrade under class imbalance and non-IID client data, both of which commonly arise in AMC due to variability in spectrum conditions and deployment settings. These challenges are further exacerbated by the scarcity of labeled data and the relative abundance of unlabeled I/Q streams in practical wireless systems.

An early deep-learning approach to AMC [39] transforms I/Q sequences into time-frequency images, including Smoothed Pseudo Wigner-Ville and Born-Jordan distributions, and applies convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to fuse them with handcrafted features. LightAMC [36] improves the efficiency of such frameworks through compressive-sensing-based pruning of CNN models. SplitAMC [23] transmits intermediate activations (“smashed data”) and gradients instead of raw signals to reduce latency and improve robustness. To address class imbalance, [9] augments underrepresented classes and combines CNNs with LSTMs for temporal modeling.

Federated learning methods for AMC include FedeAMC [33], which employs a balanced cross-entropy loss to mitigate class imbalance, and FedBKD [25], which uses bidirectional knowledge distillation to address data and model heterogeneity. Other approaches include federated incremental learning with private local classes [26] and personalized FL based on MetaSGD [29, 18], which optimizes client-specific learning rates. Several complementary lines of work focus on communication-efficient FL over wireless networks. For example, [3] surveys methods for reducing uplink and downlink costs; [24] exploits correlations between gradient subspaces to compress local updates; [28] uses unsourced massive access and approximate message passing for over-the-air model aggregation; and [11] develops schedule-aware FL over mixed terrestrial-satellite links with heterogeneous latency and bandwidth.

While these works investigate model compression and/or personalization, none explore self-supervised representation learning for AMC in federated settings. Self-supervised learning (SSL) is a natural fit for RF signal inference because labeled data are scarce while unlabeled I/Q sequences are abundant. Prior centralized studies have shown strong promise for SSL-based AMC [20, 38]. In federated settings, SSL not only reduces reliance on labeled data but can also mitigate distribution drift among heterogeneous clients [42, 4]. Building on these insights, we develop a federated self-supervised approach for AMC in realistic deployment settings.

Specifically, to address the limitations of supervised FL under label scarcity and data heterogeneity, we propose a federated self-supervised framework for AMC on distributed I/Q data. Our approach, FedSSL-AMC, collaboratively pretrains a shared encoder on unlabeled I/Q streams using a contrastive objective, promoting consistent latent representations across clients. A causal, time-dilated CNN serves as the backbone, capturing long-range temporal dependencies in modulation patterns. To limit annotation and communication overhead, each client trains a lightweight support vector machine locally using a small labeled set.

Key components of our approach and contributions include:

  • •

    Self-supervised pretraining with lightweight adaptation: We develop a causal, time-dilated CNN trained via federated averaging using a triplet-loss objective on unlabeled I/Q sequences. Each client then fits a lightweight support vector machine (SVM) on its own labeled subset for personalized classification. While similar federated SSL schemes with SVM heads have been proposed in other domains, this is the first demonstration of their effectiveness for modulation classification.

  • •

    Theoretical analysis: We provide convergence guarantees for a proximal variant of the federated self-supervised encoder trained on noisy signals, characterizing how signal noise, client heterogeneity, and inexact local updates affect descent of the global objective. For smooth encoder activations, the noise-dependent terms vanish as the SNR increases. For the downstream classifier, we derive a separability condition that quantifies the SNR required for reliable classification.

  • •

    Empirical results: We benchmark FedSSL-AMC on both synthetic and over-the-air AMC datasets. It outperforms supervised FL baselines across all three datasets and nearly all evaluated settings, including heterogeneous SNRs, carrier-frequency offsets, and non-IID label partitions.

  • •

    Resource footprint: We quantify model size, MFLOPs, and communication-round requirements, characterizing the tradeoff between classification accuracy, local computation, and communication cost.

To our knowledge, this is the first work to develop a self-supervised learning (SSL) framework for automatic modulation classification in a federated setting. The proposed approach addresses key challenges in cognitive wireless systems, including label scarcity, client heterogeneity, and privacy constraints, that centralized SSL methods are not well-suited to handle. While our primary focus is representation learning under heterogeneous and label-sparse conditions, FedSSL-AMC also reduces the number of communication rounds required during training. Consistent with prior observations that larger local datasets can improve FL efficiency [37], our experiments in Section IV-B show that, on the synthetic dataset, FedSSL-AMC achieves higher accuracy than the supervised FL baselines using 10 communication rounds, compared with the 1,000-round protocol adopted from FedeAMC, at the expense of greater local computation per round.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the proposed FedSSL-AMC framework. Section III presents the theoretical analysis of encoder convergence and downstream separability under noise and distribution shift. Section IV reports experimental results on synthetic and over-the-air datasets, and Section V concludes the paper.11 1 A preliminary version of this work appeared in the 2025 IEEE Workshop on Signal Processing Advances in Wireless Communications (SPAWC) [2]. This journal version substantially extends the workshop paper through new theoretical results, a generalized framework, and additional experiments.

II Federated Self-Supervised Learning for AMC

The proposed method addresses two major challenges in federated AMC: non-IID data across clients and limited access to labeled I/Q samples. To address both, we decouple representation learning from downstream classification: a shared encoder is pretrained on unlabeled data through federated self-supervised learning, after which each client locally trains a lightweight classifier on a small labeled subset.

II-A Representation learning on I/Q sequences

To learn representations from I/Q sequences, we map each time-series input in ℝ2×T\mathbb{R}^{2\times T} to a compact feature vector in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, where ideally d≪2​Td\ll 2T. We adopt the self-supervised time-series representation learning framework of [8], which uses a causal convolutional neural network with time dilation. The encoder architecture, illustrated in Fig. 1, consists of stacked convolutional layers in which a neuron in the kthk^{\text{th}} layer connects to neurons in the preceding layer with spacing 2k−12^{k-1}. This exponentially dilated causal design offers the following benefits:

  1. 1.

    Long-range temporal modeling. Exponentially dilated causal convolutions capture long-range dependencies through an expanded receptive field.

  2. 2.

    Scalability and efficiency. The CNN architecture supports efficient parallelization and scales to long sequences.

  3. 3.

    Online inference capability. The causal structure ensures that adding a new input element at test time requires recomputing only a small portion of the computational graph, enabling efficient online deployment.

As shown in [8], self-supervised representation learning for time-series data can be achieved using a contrastive triplet loss. Motivated by word2vec [22], the main idea is to bring similar samples closer in the feature space while pushing dissimilar ones apart. Specifically, for each randomly sampled reference sample, a positive sample should lie close in the learned embedding space, while KK negative samples should be far from it. Formally, let f⁡(x,Θ)f(x;\Theta) denote the representation of input xx produced by a deep encoder parameterized by Θ\Theta. Omitting the parameterization for brevity, the triplet loss is

ℒ⁡(xr​e​f,xp​o​s,{xkn​e​g}k=1K)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(x^{ref},x^{pos},\{x^{neg}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}) =−log⁡(σ⁡(f​(xr​e​f)T​f​(xp​o​s)))\displaystyle=-\log\left(\sigma\left(f(x^{ref})^{T}f(x^{pos})\right)\right)
−∑k=1Klog(σ(−f(xr​e​f)Tf(xkn​e​g))),\displaystyle\!\!\!-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\log\left(\sigma\left(-f(x^{ref})^{T}f(x^{neg}_{k})\right)\right), (1)

where σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid function. The loss encourages the inner product between f⁡(xr​e​f)f(x^{ref}) and f⁡(xp​o​s)f(x^{pos}) to be large and positive, while penalizing similarity with each f⁡(xkn​e​g)f(x^{neg}_{k}). When f​(xr​e​f)T​f​(xp​o​s)≫1f(x^{ref})^{T}f(x^{pos})\gg 1, the first term vanishes, i.e.,

log⁡(σ⁡(f​(xr​e​f)T​f​(xp​o​s)))≈0.\log\left(\sigma(f(x^{ref})^{T}f(x^{pos}))\right)\approx 0.

Similarly, when f​(xr​e​f)T​f​(xkn​e​g)≪−1f(x^{ref})^{T}f(x^{neg}_{k})\ll-1, it holds that

log⁡(σ⁡(−f​(xr​e​f)T​f​(xkn​e​g)))≈0.\log\left(\sigma(-f(x^{ref})^{T}f(x^{neg}_{k}))\right)\approx 0.

Thus, minimizing the triplet loss aligns related samples while separating unrelated ones in the learned representation space.

In our implementation, xp​o​sx^{pos} is a randomly sampled subsequence from the same I/Q sequence as xr​e​fx^{ref}, while each xkn​e​gx^{neg}_{k} is drawn from a different I/Q sequence. This construction exploits the local temporal consistency of wireless signals, since segments from the same sequence are more likely to share modulation patterns, and enables the model to learn meaningful representations without labels.

II-B Federated self-supervised learning

Self-supervised learning addresses limited labeled data by decoupling representation learning from downstream classification. In the federated setting, clients collaboratively train a shared feature encoder using standard federated averaging (FedAvg) [21] without exchanging raw I/Q data, and then train lightweight classifiers locally on small labeled subsets. This forms the basis of FedSSL-AMC, which combines federated self-supervised representation learning with client-specific classification under class imbalance and data heterogeneity. We use a time-dilated causal CNN as the encoder and train it on unlabeled I/Q streams using the triplet loss in (1). After encoder training, each client fits a support vector machine (SVM) on its labeled data. Algorithm 1 summarizes the full procedure.

III Analysis of Contrastive Encoder Training

This section provides theoretical guarantees for the proposed federated self-supervised learning framework. We first establish that the causal CNN encoder is Lipschitz continuous with respect to both its input signals and model parameters (Section III-A), which allows us to bound the sensitivity of the contrastive loss to additive channel noise. We then characterize how the expected gradient norm scales with the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), quantifying the effect of noise on encoder training. For analytical tractability, the convergence analysis considers a proximal variant of the local contrastive objective rather than the FedAvg implementation in Algorithm 1. Under full client participation, we characterize how signal noise, client heterogeneity, and inexact local updates affect descent of the corresponding global objective, with tighter SNR-dependent guarantees obtained for smooth encoder activations. Finally, in Section III-B, we derive a separability condition for the downstream SVM classifier trained on noisy encoder features.

III-A Convergence analysis of representation learning

We begin by introducing the notation and assumptions used to analyze the federated self-supervised representation learning process. Let us denote the input sequence length by TT and the output length at the lthl^{\text{th}} encoder layer by TlT_{l}. Let PP and γ\gamma denote the expected signal power per channel and the SNR, respectively. The following assumptions ensure that the encoder output remains bounded and make the analysis tractable.

Assumption 1.

The magnitude of every encoder weight is bounded by a constant RR.

We analyze the proposed federated self-supervised framework with a causal CNN encoder using either ReLU or Softplus activations. The analysis considers contrastive triplet-loss training under heterogeneous client data and noisy signal conditions. Using Lipschitz continuity of the encoder and bounds on the noise-induced gradient perturbation, we characterize how signal noise, client heterogeneity, and inexact local updates affect descent of the global objective for the proximal variant considered in the analysis.

III-A1 Results for a causal CNN encoder with ReLU activation

For the causal CNN encoder trained with triplet loss and ReLU activation, we derive bounds on the expected gradient norm as a function of the SNR. Building on these results, we adapt the convergence analysis of [16] to the proximal variant introduced in Section III, characterizing descent of the global objective under full client participation, noisy signals, and client heterogeneity. Full proofs are deferred to the supplementary material. We begin with the following assumptions.

Assumption 2.

The magnitude of each encoder input channel is clipped at ζ​P\zeta\sqrt{P}, where ζ∈ℝ+⁣+\zeta\in\mathbb{R}_{++} and PP denotes the expected signal power per channel.

Assumption 3.

The encoder is a Ψ\Psi-layer causal CNN with kernel size χ\chi, unit stride, c^\hat{c} channels per layer, and ReLU activations.

It bounds the expected ℓ2\ell_{2} norms of the gradients at a given SNR γ\gamma, where the expectation is taken over the additive signal noise.

So far, we have characterized how noise perturbations in the encoder input affect the gradient norms. We next analyze the effect of SNR on the convergence of the global contrastive objective in a federated setting with heterogeneous client data. This analysis requires regularity of the local objectives with respect to the encoder parameters.

Assumption 5.

For every client cc, the local objective ℒc​(Θ)\mathcal{L}_{c}(\Theta) is LlossallL_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\mathrm{all}}-smooth with respect to the encoder parameter vector Θ\Theta, i.e.,

‖∇ℒc​(Θ)−∇ℒc​(Θ′)‖2≤Llossall​‖Θ−Θ′‖2\|\nabla\mathcal{L}_{c}(\Theta)-\nabla\mathcal{L}_{c}(\Theta^{\prime})\|_{2}\leq L_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\mathrm{all}}\|\Theta-\Theta^{\prime}\|_{2}

for all Θ\Theta and Θ′\Theta^{\prime}. In addition, there exists a constant L−>0L_{-}>0 such that every local objective ℒc\mathcal{L}_{c} is L−L_{-}-weakly convex. Equivalently, wherever the Hessian exists,

∇2ℒc​(Θ)⪰−L−​I,\nabla^{2}\mathcal{L}_{c}(\Theta)\succeq-L_{-}I,

where II denotes the identity matrix.

Many existing convergence analyses, including [17], assume strong convexity of the objective. This assumption is not appropriate here because neural encoders and contrastive objectives are generally nonconvex. We therefore build on the FedProx convergence framework [16], which introduces a proximal term in each local objective to control client drift under heterogeneous data. Although our experiments use standard federated averaging for encoder training, the analysis applies to the corresponding FedProx-style variant. The resulting guarantees therefore characterize a closely related proximal implementation rather than Algorithm 1 directly.

For the federated analysis, we assume full client participation. At communication round tt, client cc minimizes the regularized local objective

hc​(Θ,Θt)=ℒc​(Θ)+μprox2​‖Θ−Θt‖22,\displaystyle h_{c}(\Theta,\Theta^{t})=\mathcal{L}_{c}(\Theta)+\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{prox}}}{2}\|\Theta-\Theta^{t}\|_{2}^{2}, (18)

where μprox>0\mu_{\mathrm{prox}}>0 controls the deviation of the local model from the current global model Θt\Theta^{t}. The corresponding local update is

Θ^ct+1=arg⁡minΘ​hc​(Θ,Θt).\displaystyle\hat{\Theta}_{c}^{t+1}=\arg\min_{\Theta}h_{c}(\Theta,\Theta^{t}). (19)

We define the local objective ℒc​(Θ)\mathcal{L}_{c}(\Theta) as the expected contrastive loss under client cc’s data distribution and additive noise:

ℒc​(Θ)=𝔼x∼𝒟c,n​[ℒ⁡(Θ,x+n)].\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{c}(\Theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{c},\,n}\big[\mathcal{L}(\Theta;x+n)\big]. (20)

Here, x={xref,xpos,x1neg,…,xKneg}x=\{x^{\mathrm{ref}},x^{\mathrm{pos}},x^{\mathrm{neg}}_{1},\dots,x^{\mathrm{neg}}_{K}\} is drawn from the local distribution 𝒟c\mathcal{D}_{c}, and n={nref,npos,n1neg,…,nKneg}n=\{n^{\mathrm{ref}},n^{\mathrm{pos}},n^{\mathrm{neg}}_{1},\dots,n^{\mathrm{neg}}_{K}\} denotes additive Gaussian noise applied independently to the samples in the triplet. The notation ℒ⁡(Θ,x+n)\mathcal{L}(\Theta;x+n) is shorthand for

ℒ⁡(f⁡(xref+nref,Θ),f⁡(xpos+npos,Θ),{f⁡(xkneg+nkneg,Θ)}k=1K).\mathcal{L}\big(f(x^{\mathrm{ref}}+n^{\mathrm{ref}};\Theta),f(x^{\mathrm{pos}}+n^{\mathrm{pos}};\Theta),\{f(x_{k}^{\mathrm{neg}}+n_{k}^{\mathrm{neg}};\Theta)\}_{k=1}^{K}\big).

We also define the corresponding clean local objective as

ℒcclean​(Θ)=𝔼x∼𝒟c​[ℒ⁡(Θ,x)],\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{c}^{\mathrm{clean}}(\Theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{c}}\big[\mathcal{L}(\Theta;x)\big], (21)

where ℒ⁡(Θ,x)\mathcal{L}(\Theta;x) denotes the same triplet loss evaluated on uncorrupted inputs. The clean global objective is

ℒglobal​(Θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{global}}(\Theta) =∑c=1Cpc​ℒcclean​(Θ)=𝔼c​[ℒcclean​(Θ)].\displaystyle=\sum_{c=1}^{C}p_{c}\,\mathcal{L}_{c}^{\mathrm{clean}}(\Theta)=\mathbb{E}_{c}\big[\mathcal{L}_{c}^{\mathrm{clean}}(\Theta)\big]. (22)

The weights satisfy pc≥0p_{c}\geq 0 and ∑c=1Cpc=1\sum_{c=1}^{C}p_{c}=1; under uniform client weighting, pc=1/Cp_{c}=1/C. If each local objective is LlossallL_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\mathrm{all}}-smooth, then their weighted average is also LlossallL_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\mathrm{all}}-smooth.

Our goal is to characterize, under full client participation, how signal noise, client heterogeneity, and inexact local updates affect descent of the clean global objective. To this end, we adopt a reformulation based on the FedProx analysis of [16], which accommodates nonconvex local objectives through proximal regularization.

Assumption 6.

Let ηie∈[0,1]\eta_{\mathrm{ie}}\in[0,1] denote the inexactness level. At communication round tt, each client computes a local solution Θct+1\Theta_{c}^{t+1} satisfying

‖∇hc​(Θct+1,Θt)‖2≤ηie​‖∇hc​(Θt,Θt)‖2.\left\|\nabla h_{c}(\Theta_{c}^{t+1},\Theta^{t})\right\|_{2}\leq\eta_{\mathrm{ie}}\left\|\nabla h_{c}(\Theta^{t},\Theta^{t})\right\|_{2}.

The server then averages the local solutions to obtain the next global iterate:

Θt+1=1C​∑c=1CΘct+1.\displaystyle\Theta^{t+1}=\frac{1}{C}\sum_{c=1}^{C}\Theta_{c}^{t+1}. (23)

We next define local dissimilarity. The clean local objectives are BdissB_{\mathrm{diss}}-locally dissimilar at Θ\Theta if

𝔼c​[‖∇ℒcclean​(Θ)‖22]≤Bdiss2​‖∇ℒglobal​(Θ)‖22.\mathbb{E}_{c}\!\left[\left\|\nabla\mathcal{L}_{c}^{\mathrm{clean}}(\Theta)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]\leq B_{\mathrm{diss}}^{2}\left\|\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{global}}(\Theta)\right\|_{2}^{2}.

This condition bounds the heterogeneity of the client gradients relative to the global gradient. We can now state the convergence result under full client participation and bounded local dissimilarity.

Theorem 2.

Assume that the clean local objectives are BdissB_{\text{diss}}-locally dissimilar at Θt\Theta^{t} , and that

Bdiss​ηie<1.B_{\mathrm{diss}}\eta_{\mathrm{ie}}<1.

Then for any SNR γ\gamma, signal power PP, and heterogeneous client data distributions, there exists a sufficiently large proximal coefficient μprox>L−\mu_{\text{prox}}>L_{-} such that

ℒglobal​(Θt+1)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{global}}(\Theta^{t+1}) ≤ℒglobal​(Θt)−𝒪⁡(1μprox)​‖∇ℒglobal​(Θt)‖22\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{L}_{\text{global}}(\Theta^{t})-\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\mu_{\text{prox}}}\right)\|\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\text{global}}(\Theta^{t})\|^{2}_{2} (24)
+𝒪(1μprox)⋅Err(γ,P,Bdiss,ηie,Θt),\displaystyle\quad+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\mu_{\text{prox}}}\right)\cdot\mathrm{Err}(\gamma,P,B_{\text{diss}},\eta_{\text{ie}},\Theta^{t}), (25)

where the error term captures the effects of signal noise, client heterogeneity, and inexact local updates. Its full expression is provided in the supplementary material.

III-A2 Results for a causal CNN encoder with Softplus activation

The bounds in Theorems 1 and 2 contain additive terms that do not depend on the SNR. This looseness arises because, with ReLU activations, the encoder Jacobian is not generally Lipschitz continuous with respect to the input. By replacing ReLU with a smooth activation such as Softplus, we can obtain tighter bounds in which these SNR-independent terms are eliminated. The following lemma formalizes the required Jacobian regularity.

Lemma 5.

Suppose the activation function is Softplus, or another twice continuously differentiable function with bounded first and second derivatives. Under the preceding bounded-input and bounded-parameter assumptions, the Jacobian of the encoder f⁡(x,θ¯1,…,θ¯Ψ)f(x;\bar{\theta}_{1},\ldots,\bar{\theta}_{\Psi}) with respect to θ¯l\bar{\theta}_{l} is ΓJ\Gamma_{J}-Lipschitz in xx for some constant ΓJ>0\Gamma_{J}>0; that is,

‖Jθ¯l​(x)−Jθ¯l​(x′)‖2≤ΓJ​‖x−x′‖2.\left\|J_{\bar{\theta}_{l}}(x)-J_{\bar{\theta}_{l}}(x^{\prime})\right\|_{2}\leq\Gamma_{J}\left\|x-x^{\prime}\right\|_{2}.

Since Softplus is also 11-Lipschitz, as is ReLU, the preceding Lipschitz and boundedness results remain applicable. Together with Lemma 5, this allows us to derive the following theorems. Their proofs closely follow those of Theorems 1 and 2 and are provided in the supplementary material.

Theorem 3.

Suppose the encoder uses Softplus, or another activation function satisfying the conditions of Lemma 5. Let zr​e​f′z^{ref^{\prime}}, zp​o​s′z^{pos^{\prime}}, {zkn​e​g′}k=1K\{z^{neg^{\prime}}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} denote the noise-perturbed embeddings, and zr​e​f,zp​o​s,{zkn​e​g}k=1Kz^{ref},z^{pos},\{z^{neg}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} their noiseless counterparts. Then the excess terms in the expected gradient-norm bounds scale as 𝒪(γ−1/2P1/2)\mathcal{O}(\gamma^{-1/2}P^{1/2}), while those in the expected squared-gradient-norm bounds scale as 𝒪⁡(γ−1​P)\mathcal{O}(\gamma^{-1}P). Specifically,

𝔼⁡[‖∇θ¯lℒ​(zr​e​f′,zp​o​s′,{zkn​e​g′})‖2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\big\|\nabla_{\bar{\theta}_{l}}\mathcal{L}(z^{ref^{\prime}},z^{pos^{\prime}},\{z^{neg^{\prime}}_{k}\})\big\|_{2}\Big]
≤‖∇θ¯lℒ​(zr​e​f,zp​o​s,{zkn​e​g})‖2+(K+2)​ΓJ​G​T​γ−1​P\displaystyle\leq\big\|\nabla_{\bar{\theta}_{l}}\mathcal{L}(z^{ref},z^{pos},\{z^{neg}_{k}\})\big\|_{2}+(K+2)\Gamma_{J}G\sqrt{T\gamma^{-1}P}
+Lθ​(l)​Γ​Lx​T​(K+2)3​γ−1​P,\displaystyle\quad+L_{\theta}(l)\Gamma L_{x}\sqrt{T(K+2)^{3}\gamma^{-1}P}, (26)
𝔼⁡[‖∇θ¯lℒ​(zr​e​f′,zp​o​s′,{zkn​e​g′})‖22]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\big\|\nabla_{\bar{\theta}_{l}}\mathcal{L}(z^{ref^{\prime}},z^{pos^{\prime}},\{z^{neg^{\prime}}_{k}\})\big\|_{2}^{2}\Big]
≤2​‖∇θ¯lℒ​(zr​e​f,zp​o​s,{zkn​e​g})‖22+4​T​γ−1​P​(K+2)2​ΓJ2​G2\displaystyle\leq\color[rgb]{0,0,0}2\big\|\nabla_{\bar{\theta}_{l}}\mathcal{L}(z^{ref},z^{pos},\{z^{neg}_{k}\})\big\|_{2}^{2}+4T\gamma^{-1}P(K+2)^{2}\Gamma_{J}^{2}G^{2}
+4​Lθ​(l)2​Γ2​Lx2​T​(K+2)3​γ−1​P,\displaystyle\quad+4L_{\theta}(l)^{2}\Gamma^{2}L_{x}^{2}T(K+2)^{3}\gamma^{-1}P, (27)
𝔼⁡[‖∇Θℒ​(zr​e​f′,zp​o​s′,{zkn​e​g′})‖2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\big\|\nabla_{\Theta}\mathcal{L}(z^{ref^{\prime}},z^{pos^{\prime}},\{z^{neg^{\prime}}_{k}\})\big\|_{2}\Big]
≤‖∇Θℒ​(zr​e​f,zp​o​s,{zkn​e​g})‖2+(K+2)​ΓJ​G​Ψ​T​γ−1​P\displaystyle\leq\big\|\nabla_{\Theta}\mathcal{L}(z^{ref},z^{pos},\{z^{neg}_{k}\})\big\|_{2}+(K+2)\Gamma_{J}G\Psi\sqrt{T\gamma^{-1}P}
+ΓLxT​(K+2)3​γ−1​P∑l=1ΨLθ(l),\displaystyle\quad+\Gamma L_{x}\sqrt{T(K+2)^{3}\gamma^{-1}P}\sum_{l=1}^{\Psi}L_{\theta}(l), (28)
𝔼⁡[‖∇Θℒ​(zr​e​f′,zp​o​s′,{zkn​e​g′})‖22]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\big\|\nabla_{\Theta}\mathcal{L}(z^{ref^{\prime}},z^{pos^{\prime}},\{z^{neg^{\prime}}_{k}\})\big\|_{2}^{2}\Big]
≤2​‖∇Θℒ​(zr​e​f,zp​o​s,{zkn​e​g})‖22+4​T​γ−1​P​(K+2)2​Ψ​ΓJ2​G2\displaystyle\leq\color[rgb]{0,0,0}2\big\|\nabla_{\Theta}\mathcal{L}(z^{ref},z^{pos},\{z^{neg}_{k}\})\big\|_{2}^{2}+4T\gamma^{-1}P(K+2)^{2}\Psi\Gamma_{J}^{2}G^{2}
+4Γ2Lx2T(K+2)3γ−1P∑l=1ΨLθ(l)2.\displaystyle\quad+4\Gamma^{2}L_{x}^{2}T(K+2)^{3}\gamma^{-1}P\sum_{l=1}^{\Psi}L_{\theta}(l)^{2}. (29)

Theorem 3 shows that, with smooth activations, the gradient deviations induced by noise admit tighter bounds than in the ReLU case. Specifically, the excess first-order terms scale as 𝒪(γ−1/2P1/2)\mathcal{O}(\gamma^{-1/2}P^{1/2}), while the excess second-order terms scale as 𝒪⁡(γ−1​P)\mathcal{O}(\gamma^{-1}P), owing to the Lipschitz continuity of the encoder Jacobians. This leads to the following convergence guarantee for noisy federated training with smooth activations.

Theorem 4.

Assume that the clean local objectives are BdissB_{\mathrm{diss}}-locally dissimilar at Θt\Theta^{t}, and that Bdiss​ηie<1B_{\mathrm{diss}}\eta_{\mathrm{ie}}<1. Then for any signal power PP and heterogeneous client data distributions, there exist a sufficiently large proximal coefficient μprox>L−\mu_{\mathrm{prox}}>L_{-} and a sufficiently large SNR γ\gamma such that

ℒglobal​(Θt+1)≤ℒglobal​(Θt)−𝒪⁡(1μprox)​‖∇ℒglobal​(Θt)‖22\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{global}}(\Theta^{t+1})\leq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{global}}(\Theta^{t})-\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\mu_{\mathrm{prox}}}\right)\|\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{global}}(\Theta^{t})\|_{2}^{2}
+𝒪(1μprox)⋅𝒪(γ−1/2P1/2)∥∇ℒglobal(Θt)∥2\displaystyle\quad+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\mu_{\mathrm{prox}}}\right)\cdot\mathcal{O}\left(\gamma^{-1/2}P^{1/2}\right)\|\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{global}}(\Theta^{t})\|_{2}
+𝒪(1μprox)⋅𝒪(γ−1P).\displaystyle\quad+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\mu_{\mathrm{prox}}}\right)\cdot\mathcal{O}\left(\gamma^{-1}P\right). (30)

The hidden constants depend on the client heterogeneity and inexactness level, while the explicit SNR-dependent terms quantify the effect of signal noise. The full expression is provided in the supplementary material.

The preceding results lead to three observations. First, Theorem 3 shows that, as γ→∞\gamma\to\infty, the excess terms in the noisy gradient-norm bounds vanish, so the bounds approach their clean-signal counterparts. Second, in the same high-SNR regime, Theorem 4 recovers the full-participation FedProx-type descent behavior of Theorem 4 in [16], whereby a sufficiently large proximal coefficient μprox\mu_{\mathrm{prox}} ensures a decrease in the global objective. Finally, because the constants in the noise-dependent bounds grow with encoder depth, channel width, and kernel size, larger architectures may require stronger proximal regularization to maintain stable descent across communication rounds.

III-B Linear separability under a hard-margin SVM

We now analyze the encoder outputs under hard-margin linear classification. In the noise-free setting, we assume that the features produced by the causal CNN encoder are (μ,ρ)(\mu,\rho)-separable. Specifically, for each input signal rqr_{q}, the corresponding feature vector ϕ⁡(rq)\phi(r_{q}) satisfies ‖ϕ⁡(rq)‖2≤ρ\|\phi(r_{q})\|_{2}\leq\rho, and the labeled dataset 𝒟={(ϕ⁡(rq),yq)}q=1Q¯\mathcal{D}=\{(\phi(r_{q}),y_{q})\}_{q=1}^{\bar{Q}} contains Q¯\bar{Q} binary-labeled examples with yq∈{+1,−1}y_{q}\in\{+1,-1\}. By definition of (μ,ρ)(\mu,\rho)-separability, there exist a unit-norm weight vector θsvm,w∗\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{svm},w} and a bias θsvm,bias∗\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{svm},\mathrm{bias}} such that

yq​(θsvm,w∗T​ϕ​(rq)+θsvm,bias∗)≥μ.y_{q}\left(\theta^{*T}_{\mathrm{svm},w}\,\phi(r_{q})+\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{svm},\mathrm{bias}}\right)\geq\mu.

In practical AMC settings, the received signals are corrupted by noise, and the resulting encoder features may no longer remain linearly separable. Let γenc\gamma_{\mathrm{enc}} denote the SNR at the encoder output, and assume that it increases monotonically with the input SNR γ\gamma. We model the noisy encoder output as ϕq=ϕ⁡(rq)+wq\phi_{q}=\phi(r_{q})+w_{q}, where ϕ⁡(rq)\phi(r_{q}) is the noise-free feature vector and wqw_{q} is zero-mean Gaussian noise satisfying

Cov⁡(wq)⪯ρ​γenc−1​I.\operatorname{Cov}(w_{q})\preceq\rho\gamma_{\mathrm{enc}}^{-1}I.

Let

w~q=θsvm,w∗T​wq.\tilde{w}_{q}=\theta_{\mathrm{svm},w}^{*T}w_{q}.

The signed margin of the noisy feature under the clean-data separating hyperplane is

yq​(θsvm,w∗T​ϕq+θsvm,bias∗)\displaystyle y_{q}\left(\theta_{\mathrm{svm},w}^{*T}\phi_{q}+\theta_{\mathrm{svm},\mathrm{bias}}^{*}\right) =yq​(θsvm,w∗T​ϕ​(rq)+θsvm,bias∗)+yq​w~q.\displaystyle=y_{q}\left(\theta_{\mathrm{svm},w}^{*T}\phi(r_{q})+\theta_{\mathrm{svm},\mathrm{bias}}^{*}\right)+y_{q}\tilde{w}_{q}. (31)

Since the clean signed margin is at least μ\mu, the noisy feature remains correctly separated whenever

yq​w~q>−μ.\displaystyle y_{q}\tilde{w}_{q}>-\mu. (32)

Because ‖θsvm,w∗‖2=1\|\theta_{\mathrm{svm},w}^{*}\|_{2}=1, w~q\tilde{w}_{q} is Gaussian with zero mean and variance bounded by

Var⁡(w~q)=θsvm,w∗T​Cov⁡(wq)​θsvm,w∗≤ρ​γenc−1.\operatorname{Var}(\tilde{w}_{q})=\theta_{\mathrm{svm},w}^{*T}\operatorname{Cov}(w_{q})\theta_{\mathrm{svm},w}^{*}\leq\rho\gamma_{\mathrm{enc}}^{-1}.

Assuming that the noise vectors are independent across samples, the probability that all noisy features remain correctly separated by the clean-data hyperplane satisfies

Pr⁡(yq​(θsvm,w∗T​ϕq+θsvm,bias∗)>0,∀q)\displaystyle\Pr\left(y_{q}\left(\theta_{\mathrm{svm},w}^{*T}\phi_{q}+\theta_{\mathrm{svm},\mathrm{bias}}^{*}\right)>0,\ \forall q\right)
≥[1−Q⁡(μρ​γenc−1)]Q¯.\displaystyle\geq\left[1-Q\left(\frac{\mu}{\sqrt{\rho\gamma_{\mathrm{enc}}^{-1}}}\right)\right]^{\bar{Q}}. (33)

This leads to the following guarantee.

Theorem 5.

Let 𝒟={(ϕ⁡(rq),yq)}q=1Q¯\mathcal{D}=\{(\phi(r_{q}),y_{q})\}_{q=1}^{\bar{Q}} be a clean dataset that is (μ,ρ)(\mu,\rho)-separable under the causal CNN encoder. Assume that the feature-noise vectors are independent across samples. Then, for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exists a threshold δ⁡(ϵ,Q¯)>0\delta(\epsilon,\bar{Q})>0 such that, if γenc>δ⁡(ϵ,Q¯)\gamma_{\mathrm{enc}}>\delta(\epsilon,\bar{Q}), all samples in the noisy dataset 𝒟′={(ϕq,yq)}q=1Q¯\mathcal{D}^{\prime}=\{(\phi_{q},y_{q})\}_{q=1}^{\bar{Q}} are correctly separated by the clean-data hyperplane with probability at least 1−ϵ1-\epsilon.

Proof. From the preceding bound, the probability that all noisy samples remain correctly separated by the clean-data hyperplane satisfies

Pr⁡(yq​(θsvm,w∗T​ϕq+θsvm,bias∗)>0,∀q)≥[1−Q⁡(μρ​γenc−1)]Q¯.\Pr\left(y_{q}\left(\theta_{\mathrm{svm},w}^{*T}\phi_{q}+\theta_{\mathrm{svm},\mathrm{bias}}^{*}\right)>0,\ \forall q\right)\geq\left[1-Q\left(\frac{\mu}{\sqrt{\rho\gamma_{\mathrm{enc}}^{-1}}}\right)\right]^{\bar{Q}}.

As γenc→∞\gamma_{\mathrm{enc}}\to\infty, the argument of the QQ-function tends to infinity, and hence the lower bound tends to 11. Therefore, for any fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exists a finite threshold δ⁡(ϵ,Q¯)\delta(\epsilon,\bar{Q}) such that the probability is at least 1−ϵ1-\epsilon whenever γenc>δ⁡(ϵ,Q¯)\gamma_{\mathrm{enc}}>\delta(\epsilon,\bar{Q}). ■\blacksquare

IV Experimental Results

IV-A Experimental settings

We evaluate FedSSL-AMC against seven supervised learning baselines and four self-supervised learning baselines. The supervised baselines are:

  • •

    FedeAMC-CNN [33] addresses class imbalance using class-weighted cross-entropy. It employs the CNN architecture in Table I, which is also used by all supervised baselines for a consistent comparison.

  • •

    PMSGD-CNN [29] selects a client-specific learning rate through a grid search to mitigate data heterogeneity. Each client evaluates learning rates in {0.01,0.001,0.0001}\{0.01,0.001,0.0001\} using 20%20\% of its training samples and selects the value yielding the lowest training loss.

  • •

    FedAvg-CNN denotes standard federated averaging.

  • •

    FedProx-CNN [16] adds the proximal term μprox2​‖θlocal−θglobal‖22\frac{\mu_{\text{prox}}}{2}\|\theta_{\text{local}}-\theta_{\text{global}}\|_{2}^{2} to limit local-model drift under non-IID data. We set μprox=0.01\mu_{\text{prox}}=0.01.

  • •

    FedDyn-CNN [1] uses a dynamic regularizer to reduce mismatch between local and global objectives. We set the regularization strength to 0.010.01.

  • •

    FedAH-CNN [41] maintains both a global and a locally adapted copy of the output layer. After each local round, the two are combined through element-wise aggregation with trainable weights.

  • •

    FedRep-CNN [5] alternates between training a shared feature extractor, whose parameters are globally aggregated, and a personalized output layer that remains local. After representation training, the feature extractor is frozen and the local output layer is trained.

For the self-supervised learning baselines, we include:

  • •

    SimCSE-CNN+SVM, inspired by [10], forms positive pairs by passing the same input through dropout. Apart from this positive-pair construction, it follows the same training pipeline as FedSSL-AMC.

  • •

    SemiAMC [20] adapts a centralized semi-supervised contrastive AMC method to the federated setting. It uses I/Q rotation for data augmentation and combines convolutional layers with a two-layer LSTM to capture local and long-range temporal structure. As in FedSSL-AMC, the encoder is frozen after representation learning.

  • •

    DAE [14] adapts an LSTM-based denoising autoencoder for centralized AMC to the federated setting. Representation learning minimizes reconstruction loss, while the subsequent labeled-data phase minimizes a weighted combination of reconstruction and cross-entropy losses. To remain faithful to the original method, the encoder is not frozen during this second phase.

  • •

    CSSL-AMC [7] adapts a centralized self-supervised contrastive AMC method to distributed settings. It augments high SNR data with additive Gaussian noise and uses ResNet-18. We report the original protocol, CSSL-AMC (Enc. not frozen), which performs end-to-end fine-tuning after representation learning, and CSSL-AMC (Enc. frozen), which freezes the encoder while training the classifier on labeled data. The frozen encoder variant enables a protocol-consistent comparison with SemiAMC and FedSSL-AMC, which evaluate pretrained representations with limited downstream adaptation.

Of the eleven baselines above, FedeAMC-CNN, PMSGD-CNN, CSSL-AMC, SemiAMC, and DAE were originally proposed for automatic modulation classification, and only FedeAMC-CNN and PMSGD-CNN were designed for federated learning. The remaining methods are our adaptations for the distributed AMC setting.

Across all experiments, FedSSL-AMC uses a 10-layer causal CNN encoder with kernel size 3 and a 320-dimensional output representation. During contrastive training, each anchor is paired with one positive and 10 negative samples. For FedSSL-AMC and all self-supervised baselines, representation learning runs for Trounds=10T_{\text{rounds}}=10 communication rounds. In each round, clients perform 15,000 local training steps with batch size 50 using Adam [15] and a learning rate of 0.001.

Datasets. We evaluate the framework on three datasets.

  • •

    Custom synthetic dataset: Following the signal model in [33], we generate a synthetic dataset with received baseband signal

    r⁡[n]=A​ej⁡(Δ​θ+2​π​Δ​f​nN)​s​[n]+w⁡[n],\displaystyle r[n]=Ae^{j(\Delta\theta+2\pi\Delta f\frac{n}{N})}s[n]+w[n], (34)

    where s⁡[n]s[n] is the transmitted symbol at time index nn, AA is the channel gain, Δ​θ\Delta\theta is the carrier phase offset, Δ​f\Delta f is the normalized carrier-frequency offset, and NN is the number of I/Q symbols per sequence. The additive noise w⁡[n]w[n] is circularly symmetric complex Gaussian. For each sequence, we draw A0∼Rayleigh⁡(1)A_{0}\sim\operatorname{Rayleigh}(1) and set A=min⁡{A0,1}A=\min\{A_{0},1\}, while Δ​θ∼𝒰⁡(0,π/16)\Delta\theta\sim\mathcal{U}(0,\pi/16) and Δ​f=0.01\Delta f=0.01. The signal-to-noise ratio is

    SNR=10​log10⁡(∑n=0N−1|A​ej⁡(Δ​θ+2​π​Δ​f​nN)​s​[n]|2∑n=0N−1|w⁡[n]|2),\displaystyle\text{SNR}=10\log_{10}\left(\frac{\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\left|Ae^{j(\Delta\theta+2\pi\Delta f\frac{n}{N})}s[n]\right|^{2}}{\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}|w[n]|^{2}}\right), (35)

    with SNR sampled uniformly from 𝒰⁡(−10,10)\mathcal{U}(-10,10) during both training and evaluation.

    Each I/Q sequence contains N=100N=100 complex samples, and we consider four modulation types: BPSK, QPSK, 8-PSK, and 16-QAM. The federated setup includes four clients, each with 140,000140{,}000 unlabeled and 2,8002{,}800 labeled training samples. To induce label imbalance and non-IID client distributions, the modulation classes are assigned unevenly across clients. In the order [BPSK, QPSK, 8-PSK, 16-QAM], the class counts are:

    1. 1.

      Client 1: [60,000,60,000,10,000,10,000][60{,}000,60{,}000,10{,}000,10{,}000] unlabeled and [1,200,1,200,200,200][1{,}200,1{,}200,200,200] labeled samples.

    2. 2.

      Client 2: [10,000,60,000,60,000,10,000][10{,}000,60{,}000,60{,}000,10{,}000] unlabeled and [200,1,200,1,200,200][200,1{,}200,1{,}200,200] labeled samples.

    3. 3.

      Client 3: [10,000,10,000,60,000,60,000][10{,}000,10{,}000,60{,}000,60{,}000] unlabeled and [200,200,1,200,1,200][200,200,1{,}200,1{,}200] labeled samples.

    4. 4.

      Client 4: [60,000,10,000,10,000,60,000][60{,}000,10{,}000,10{,}000,60{,}000] unlabeled and [1,200,200,200,1,200][1{,}200,200,200,1{,}200] labeled samples.

    Following the original FedeAMC training protocol, all supervised baselines use 1,0001{,}000 communication rounds with one local epoch per client per round, a batch size of 6464, and a learning rate of 0.0010.001. We also adopt the label distribution from [33] to ensure a fair and faithful comparison with FedeAMC, the primary prior work on federated automatic modulation classification.

    Each client’s test set follows the class distribution of its labeled training data and contains one-tenth as many samples. Test SNRs are sampled independently from 𝒰⁡(−10,10)\mathcal{U}(-10,10).

  • •

    MIGOU dataset: The MIGOU dataset [32] contains over-the-air I/Q measurements from 11 modulation classes, including AM, FM, QAM, and PSK signals, transmitted using a USRP B210 and recorded at distances of 1 m and 6 m. These distances correspond to average SNRs of 37 dB and 22 dB, respectively. Its larger number of modulation classes makes MIGOU useful for evaluating robustness under label imbalance and client heterogeneity. To generate non-IID client distributions, we partition each modulation class using Dirichlet sampling:

    p⁡([x1,x2,x3,x4])=1B⁡(α)​∏i=14xiαi−1,p([x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4}])=\frac{1}{B(\alpha)}\prod_{i=1}^{4}x_{i}^{\alpha_{i}-1},

    where xix_{i} is the fraction of samples from a given class assigned to client ii, and B⁡(α)B(\alpha) is the multivariate Beta function. We set α=α¯​[1,1,1,1]\alpha=\bar{\alpha}[1,1,1,1], where smaller α¯\bar{\alpha} yields more uneven class distributions and larger values produce more uniform splits. Figure 2 shows the client-wise distributions for α¯=0.1\bar{\alpha}=0.1; distributions for other values are provided in Appendix Section B-B. In the main experiments, each client receives 140,000140{,}000 unlabeled and 2,8002{,}800 labeled samples. All methods are trained for 10 communication rounds with 100 local epochs per round.

  • •

    DeepSig 2018.01A dataset: The DeepSig 2018.01A dataset [6] contains synthetic and over-the-air recordings from 24 digital and analog modulation classes. SNR ranges from −20-20 dB to 3030 dB in 2 dB increments. For each modulation class and SNR level, the dataset provides 4,0964{,}096 examples, each consisting of 1,0241{,}024 complex I/Q samples. We consider four clients and partition each modulation class across them using the same Dirichlet procedure as for MIGOU. Each client receives 2,5002{,}500 samples per modulation class and SNR level, including 500500 labeled samples; the remainder are treated as unlabeled. As with MIGOU, supervised baselines are trained for 10 communication rounds with 100 local epochs per round.

IV-B Results

Table II reports classification accuracy across all three datasets. For MIGOU and DeepSig, we set the Dirichlet concentration parameter to α¯=0.1\bar{\alpha}=0.1 to induce substantial label heterogeneity across clients. FedSSL-AMC achieves the highest accuracy on all three datasets, demonstrating strong performance under both client heterogeneity and limited label availability.

Next, we conduct ablation studies, primarily on the custom synthetic dataset, to assess the sensitivity of FedSSL-AMC to SNR, labeled-sample size, carrier-frequency offset, model heterogeneity, and label heterogeneity.

  • •

    Number of labeled samples. We assess label efficiency on the custom synthetic dataset by varying the number of labeled samples per client and reporting client-averaged accuracy in Table III. FedeAMC is particularly sensitive to label scarcity, with accuracy dropping sharply at smaller labeled-set sizes. Fig. 3 shows confusion matrices for 14,000 labeled samples per client. FedSSL-AMC exhibits a stronger diagonal structure and fewer systematic off-diagonal errors than SimCSE-CNN+SVM and FedDyn-CNN, indicating better discrimination among modulation classes.

  • •

    Variable SNR conditions across clients. We next introduce client-level SNR heterogeneity on the custom synthetic dataset. Each client receives 14,000 labeled training sequences, with SNRs sampled from different ranges: 𝒰⁡(−10,−5)\mathcal{U}(-10,-5) for Client 1, 𝒰⁡(−5,0)\mathcal{U}(-5,0) for Client 2, 𝒰⁡(0,5)\mathcal{U}(0,5) for Client 3, and 𝒰⁡(5,10)\mathcal{U}(5,10) for Client 4. We also evaluate test accuracy as the SNR varies from −10-10 dB to 99 dB. As shown in Fig. 4, accuracy increases with SNR. Table IV further shows that the causal-CNN-based self-supervised methods outperform the supervised baselines under heterogeneous SNR conditions.

  • •

    Variation in Δ​f\Delta f. We next examine mobility-induced heterogeneity by varying the carrier-frequency offset (CFO) Δ​f\Delta f. Each client is assigned a different mobility regime, as summarized in Table V; the corresponding mapping between mobility and Δ​f\Delta f is detailed in the appendix. Figure 5 reports client-averaged test accuracy for 2,8002{,}800 and 14,00014{,}000 labeled samples per client, while Table VI presents the corresponding SNR-averaged accuracies. FedSSL-AMC generally outperforms the supervised and self-supervised baselines, although FedAH-CNN and FedRep-CNN remain competitive at lower SNRs.

  • •

    Model heterogeneity. We evaluate FedSSL-AMC under heterogeneous model precision on the custom synthetic dataset. Client 1 uses float32, Client 2 uses float16, and Clients 3 and 4 use int8 quantization during training. Figure 6 reports test accuracy with 14,00014{,}000 labeled samples per client. Despite the differences in bit width, FedSSL-AMC outperforms all baselines.

  • •

    Degree of label heterogeneity α¯\bar{\alpha}. We vary the Dirichlet concentration parameter α¯\bar{\alpha} from 0.050.05 to 1.01.0 on the MIGOU dataset to assess sensitivity to label heterogeneity. For each value, we report the mean and standard deviation of client-averaged accuracy over 10 independent runs. We also consider a larger setting with 16 clients at α¯=0.05\bar{\alpha}=0.05, organized into five clusters of sizes 3, 3, 3, 3, and 4. Because the data are distributed across more clients, each client receives 14,000 unlabeled samples. Results are reported in Table VII. Under severe heterogeneity, FedSSL-AMC generally outperforms the baselines by a clear margin, except for CSSL-AMC (Enc. not frozen), which fine-tunes the entire encoder during downstream supervised training. The large gap between the encoder-frozen and encoder-not-frozen CSSL-AMC variants indicates that much of its performance gain comes from downstream encoder adaptation rather than from the pretrained representation alone. In contrast, FedSSL-AMC remains competitive while keeping the encoder fixed and training only a lightweight classifier. Because MIGOU contains only two SNR levels, we evaluate SNR sensitivity on DeepSig for α¯∈{0.1,0.5}\bar{\alpha}\in\{0.1,0.5\}. Figure 7 shows the resulting four-client-averaged accuracy curves. Most baselines degrade under this setting, whereas FedSSL-AMC remains consistently strong and achieves slightly higher accuracy at the more heterogeneous setting, α¯=0.1\bar{\alpha}=0.1.

IV-C Complexity Analysis

Contrastive overhead and communication. The main additional computational cost of FedSSL-AMC arises from the contrastive objective, which compares each anchor with 10 negative samples. Its communication and server-side aggregation costs per round remain comparable to those of standard FL methods such as FedAvg and FedProx. FedDyn incurs additional client and server computation through its regularization and correction terms, while PMSGD, FedAH, and FedRep do not increase communication volume relative to FedAvg. However, PMSGD requires a client-side grid search over learning rates, and FedAH incurs additional local computation to train aggregation weights. The supervised baselines use 1,000 communication rounds, whereas FedSSL-AMC achieves higher accuracy in 10 rounds. This indicates substantially greater communication-round efficiency, although FedSSL-AMC performs more local computation per round. The contrastive baselines CSSL-AMC and SemiAMC have comparable algorithmic complexity when controlling for encoder architecture. However, CSSL-AMC’s augmentation strategy requires high-SNR samples, limiting its applicability when much of the training data has medium or low SNR.

Parameter count and computation. The proposed encoder has substantially fewer trainable parameters than the supervised CNN baseline (0.247M versus 1.78M), but requires more inference computation (473.56 versus 17.76 MFLOPs) because of its deeper causal, time-dilated architecture. The contrastive objective further increases training-time computation. Despite this higher computational cost, the encoder remains practical for edge deployment and offers improved use of unlabeled data together with substantially fewer communication rounds.

Encoder design. Let Ψ\Psi denote the number of 1D convolutional layers, χ\chi the kernel size, and Λ\Lambda the input sequence length. Treating the channel width as fixed, the computational complexity of the causal CNN encoder is 𝒪⁡(χ​Ψ​Λ)\mathcal{O}(\chi\Psi\Lambda). Dilated convolutions expand the receptive field without increasing the number of kernel evaluations per layer, preserving linear scaling with sequence length. By contrast, standard self-attention has quadratic complexity in Λ\Lambda, which can be less suitable for long sequences.

V Conclusion

We introduced FedSSL-AMC, a federated self-supervised framework for automatic modulation classification under heterogeneous client data and limited label availability. Our analysis establishes noise-dependent gradient bounds and convergence guarantees for a closely related proximal training variant under non-IID data, together with a high-probability separability result for the downstream classifier. Empirically, FedSSL-AMC consistently outperforms the supervised baselines, particularly when unlabeled data are abundant and labeled samples are scarce or unevenly distributed across clients.

Future work will investigate whether clustering clients by data distribution, for example through group-wise contrastive learning or adaptive aggregation, can further improve performance. The framework may also be applicable to related RF tasks such as spectrum sensing, interference classification, and waveform identification, which share challenges including distributed sensing, privacy constraints, non-IID channel conditions, limited uplink capacity, and scarce labels. In these settings, a shared causal CNN encoder could learn representations from unlabeled I/Q data, while lightweight local classifiers support adaptation to client-specific propagation environments and hardware characteristics.

Appendix Outline

This appendix provides proofs of the results omitted from the main text, together with additional modeling and dataset details.

  • •

    Section A-A proves Lemmas 1, 2, 3, and 4.

  • •

    Section A-B proves Theorem 1, which bounds the expected gradient norms under additive noise.

  • •

    Section A-C proves Theorem 2, establishing the convergence result for the proximal federated training variant.

  • •

    Section Theorem  proves the corresponding results for a causal CNN encoder with Softplus activation.

  • •

    Section B describes the mobility-induced carrier-frequency-offset model and illustrates how varying α¯\bar{\alpha} affects the client label distributions.

Appendix A Proofs of theoretical results

A-A Proofs of supporting lemmas

This subsection proves the supporting lemmas used in the main theoretical results. We begin with Lemma 1, using the following auxiliary fact: The ReLU activation is 11-Lipschitz.

Proof.

For any scalars x,x′∈ℝx,x^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R},

|ReLU⁡(x)−ReLU⁡(x′)|≤|x−x′|.\left|\operatorname{ReLU}(x)-\operatorname{ReLU}(x^{\prime})\right|\leq|x-x^{\prime}|.

Indeed, if xx and x′x^{\prime} have the same sign, the inequality follows directly. If, without loss of generality, x≥0x\geq 0 and x′<0x^{\prime}<0, then

|ReLU⁡(x)−ReLU⁡(x′)|=|x|≤|x−x′|.\left|\operatorname{ReLU}(x)-\operatorname{ReLU}(x^{\prime})\right|=|x|\leq|x-x^{\prime}|.

Since ReLU acts elementwise, summing the squared scalar inequalities over all coordinates gives

‖ReLU⁡(x)−ReLU⁡(x′)‖2≤‖x−x′‖2.\left\|\operatorname{ReLU}(x)-\operatorname{ReLU}(x^{\prime})\right\|_{2}\leq\left\|x-x^{\prime}\right\|_{2}.

Thus, ReLU is 11-Lipschitz. ∎

A-A1 Proof of Lemma 1

Lemma 1.

The encoder function f⁡(x,Θ¯1,…,Θ¯Ψ)f(x;\bar{\Theta}_{1},\dots,\bar{\Theta}_{\Psi}) is LxL_{x}-Lipschitz in xx, with Lx=(Rmat)ΨL_{x}=(R_{\mathrm{mat}})^{\Psi}; that is,

‖f⁡(x,Θ¯1,…,Θ¯Ψ)−f⁡(x′,Θ¯1,…,Θ¯Ψ)‖2≤Lx​‖x−x′‖2.\|f(x;\bar{\Theta}_{1},\dots,\bar{\Theta}_{\Psi})-f(x^{\prime};\bar{\Theta}_{1},\dots,\bar{\Theta}_{\Psi})\|_{2}\leq L_{x}\|x-x^{\prime}\|_{2}.
Proof.

Let Pad⁡(⋅)\operatorname{Pad}(\cdot) denote the zero-padding operation, so that

r¯l−1=Pad⁡(r~l−1),\bar{r}_{l-1}=\operatorname{Pad}(\tilde{r}_{l-1}),

where r~l−1\tilde{r}_{l-1} is the unpadded input to layer ll. Since zero padding preserves the Euclidean norm and ReLU is 11-Lipschitz, we can bound the Lipschitz constant of the encoder layer by layer.

We prove by induction that, for each l=1,…,Ψ−1l=1,\ldots,\Psi-1, the mapping from the encoder input to the output of layer ll is (∏i=1l‖Θ¯i‖2)(\prod_{i=1}^{l}\|\bar{\Theta}_{i}\|_{2})-Lipschitz.

Base case: For l=1l=1,

‖r~1−r~1′‖2\displaystyle\|\tilde{r}_{1}-\tilde{r}_{1}^{\prime}\|_{2} =‖ReLU⁡(Θ¯1​r¯0)−ReLU⁡(Θ¯1​r¯0′)‖2\displaystyle=\|\operatorname{ReLU}(\bar{\Theta}_{1}\bar{r}_{0})-\operatorname{ReLU}(\bar{\Theta}_{1}\bar{r}_{0}^{\prime})\|_{2}
≤‖Θ¯1​r¯0−Θ¯1​r¯0′‖2\displaystyle\leq\|\bar{\Theta}_{1}\bar{r}_{0}-\bar{\Theta}_{1}\bar{r}_{0}^{\prime}\|_{2}
=‖Θ¯1​(r¯0−r¯0′)‖2\displaystyle=\|\bar{\Theta}_{1}(\bar{r}_{0}-\bar{r}_{0}^{\prime})\|_{2}
≤‖Θ¯1‖2​‖r¯0−r¯0′‖2\displaystyle\leq\|\bar{\Theta}_{1}\|_{2}\|\bar{r}_{0}-\bar{r}_{0}^{\prime}\|_{2}
=‖Θ¯1‖2​‖Pad⁡(r~0)−Pad⁡(r~0′)‖2\displaystyle=\|\bar{\Theta}_{1}\|_{2}\|\operatorname{Pad}(\tilde{r}_{0})-\operatorname{Pad}(\tilde{r}_{0}^{\prime})\|_{2}
=‖Θ¯1‖2​‖r~0−r~0′‖2\displaystyle=\|\bar{\Theta}_{1}\|_{2}\|\tilde{r}_{0}-\tilde{r}_{0}^{\prime}\|_{2}
=‖Θ¯1‖2​‖x−x′‖2.\displaystyle=\|\bar{\Theta}_{1}\|_{2}\|x-x^{\prime}\|_{2}. (36)

Inductive step: Suppose that, for some j≥2j\geq 2,

‖r~j−1−r~j−1′‖2≤∏i=1j−1‖Θ¯i‖2​‖x−x′‖2.\|\tilde{r}_{j-1}-\tilde{r}_{j-1}^{\prime}\|_{2}\leq\prod_{i=1}^{j-1}\|\bar{\Theta}_{i}\|_{2}\|x-x^{\prime}\|_{2}.

Then

‖r~j−r~j′‖2\displaystyle\|\tilde{r}_{j}-\tilde{r}_{j}^{\prime}\|_{2} =‖ReLU⁡(Θ¯j​r¯j−1)−ReLU⁡(Θ¯j​r¯j−1′)‖2\displaystyle=\|\operatorname{ReLU}(\bar{\Theta}_{j}\bar{r}_{j-1})-\operatorname{ReLU}(\bar{\Theta}_{j}\bar{r}_{j-1}^{\prime})\|_{2}
≤‖Θ¯j​r¯j−1−Θ¯j​r¯j−1′‖2\displaystyle\leq\|\bar{\Theta}_{j}\bar{r}_{j-1}-\bar{\Theta}_{j}\bar{r}_{j-1}^{\prime}\|_{2}
=‖Θ¯j​(r¯j−1−r¯j−1′)‖2\displaystyle=\|\bar{\Theta}_{j}(\bar{r}_{j-1}-\bar{r}_{j-1}^{\prime})\|_{2}
≤‖Θ¯j‖2​‖r¯j−1−r¯j−1′‖2\displaystyle\leq\|\bar{\Theta}_{j}\|_{2}\|\bar{r}_{j-1}-\bar{r}_{j-1}^{\prime}\|_{2}
=‖Θ¯j‖2​‖Pad⁡(r~j−1)−Pad⁡(r~j−1′)‖2\displaystyle=\|\bar{\Theta}_{j}\|_{2}\|\operatorname{Pad}(\tilde{r}_{j-1})-\operatorname{Pad}(\tilde{r}_{j-1}^{\prime})\|_{2}
=‖Θ¯j‖2​‖r~j−1−r~j−1′‖2\displaystyle=\|\bar{\Theta}_{j}\|_{2}\|\tilde{r}_{j-1}-\tilde{r}_{j-1}^{\prime}\|_{2}
≤∏i=1j‖Θ¯i‖2​‖x−x′‖2.\displaystyle\leq\prod_{i=1}^{j}\|\bar{\Theta}_{i}\|_{2}\|x-x^{\prime}\|_{2}. (37)

Therefore, the mapping from the encoder input to the output of layer Ψ−1\Psi-1 is (∏i=1Ψ−1‖Θ¯i‖2)(\prod_{i=1}^{\Psi-1}\|\bar{\Theta}_{i}\|_{2})-Lipschitz. For the final layer,

‖f⁡(x,Θ¯1,…,Θ¯Ψ)−f⁡(x′,Θ¯1,…,Θ¯Ψ)‖2\displaystyle\|f(x;\bar{\Theta}_{1},\dots,\bar{\Theta}_{\Psi})-f(x^{\prime};\bar{\Theta}_{1},\dots,\bar{\Theta}_{\Psi})\|_{2}
=‖Θ¯Ψ​(r¯Ψ−1−r¯Ψ−1′)‖2\displaystyle=\|\bar{\Theta}_{\Psi}(\bar{r}_{\Psi-1}-\bar{r}_{\Psi-1}^{\prime})\|_{2}
≤‖Θ¯Ψ‖2​‖r¯Ψ−1−r¯Ψ−1′‖2\displaystyle\leq\|\bar{\Theta}_{\Psi}\|_{2}\|\bar{r}_{\Psi-1}-\bar{r}_{\Psi-1}^{\prime}\|_{2}
≤∏i=1Ψ‖Θ¯i‖2​‖x−x′‖2.\displaystyle\leq\prod_{i=1}^{\Psi}\|\bar{\Theta}_{i}\|_{2}\|x-x^{\prime}\|_{2}. (38)

Finally, Assumption 4 gives

‖Θ¯i‖2≤Rmatfor all ​i,\|\bar{\Theta}_{i}\|_{2}\leq R_{\mathrm{mat}}\qquad\text{for all }i,

and hence

‖f⁡(x,Θ¯1,…,Θ¯Ψ)−f⁡(x′,Θ¯1,…,Θ¯Ψ)‖2≤(Rmat)Ψ​‖x−x′‖2.\|f(x;\bar{\Theta}_{1},\dots,\bar{\Theta}_{\Psi})-f(x^{\prime};\bar{\Theta}_{1},\dots,\bar{\Theta}_{\Psi})\|_{2}\leq(R_{\mathrm{mat}})^{\Psi}\|x-x^{\prime}\|_{2}.

Thus, the encoder is LxL_{x}-Lipschitz in xx with Lx=(Rmat)ΨL_{x}=(R_{\mathrm{mat}})^{\Psi}. ∎

A-A2 Proofs of Lemmas 2–3 and related corollaries

To prove Lemma 2, we first establish the following bound on the layer activations.

Lemma 6 (Activation bound).

Every element of the encoder activation at layer ll is bounded in magnitude by

ζ​P​(c^​χ​R)l.\zeta\sqrt{P}\,(\hat{c}\chi R)^{l}.
Proof.

We proceed by induction on ll.

Base case: For l=1l=1, each convolutional output is the inner product of a kernel vector and an input vector, each of dimension c^​χ\hat{c}\chi. Every kernel entry is bounded in magnitude by RR, and every input entry is bounded by ζ​P\zeta\sqrt{P}. Therefore, by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,

|⟨θ,u⟩|\displaystyle\left|\left\langle\theta,u\right\rangle\right| ≤‖θ‖2​‖u‖2\displaystyle\leq\|\theta\|_{2}\|u\|_{2}
≤R​c^​χ​ζ​P​c^​χ\displaystyle\leq R\sqrt{\hat{c}\chi}\,\zeta\sqrt{P}\sqrt{\hat{c}\chi}
=ζ​P​c^​χ​R.\displaystyle=\zeta\sqrt{P}\,\hat{c}\chi R. (39)

Because ReLU does not increase the magnitude of its input, every activation at the first layer is bounded by ζ​P​(c^​χ​R)\zeta\sqrt{P}(\hat{c}\chi R).

Inductive step: Suppose that every activation at layer l−1l-1 is bounded in magnitude by

ζ​P​(c^​χ​R)l−1.\zeta\sqrt{P}\,(\hat{c}\chi R)^{l-1}.

Each pre-activation at layer ll is again an inner product of dimension c^​χ\hat{c}\chi. Its kernel entries are bounded by RR, while its input entries are bounded by ζ​P​(c^​χ​R)l−1\zeta\sqrt{P}(\hat{c}\chi R)^{l-1}. Hence,

|⟨θ,u⟩|\displaystyle\left|\left\langle\theta,u\right\rangle\right| ≤R​c^​χ​ζ​P​(c^​χ​R)l−1​c^​χ\displaystyle\leq R\sqrt{\hat{c}\chi}\,\zeta\sqrt{P}(\hat{c}\chi R)^{l-1}\sqrt{\hat{c}\chi}
=ζ​P​(c^​χ​R)l.\displaystyle=\zeta\sqrt{P}\,(\hat{c}\chi R)^{l}. (40)

Applying ReLU preserves this upper bound. The result therefore holds for every layer ll. ∎

Lemma 2.

The encoder function f⁡(x,Θ¯1,…,Θ¯Ψ)≡f⁡(x,θ¯1,…,θ¯Ψ)f(x;\bar{\Theta}_{1},\dots,\bar{\Theta}_{\Psi})\equiv f(x;\bar{\theta}_{1},\dots,\bar{\theta}_{\Psi}) is Lθ​(l)L_{\theta}(l)-Lipschitz with respect to the parameter vector θ¯l\bar{\theta}_{l}, where

Lθ​(l)=Tl​c^​χ​ζ​P​(c^​χ​R)l−1​(Rmat)Ψ−l.L_{\theta}(l)=\sqrt{T_{l}\hat{c}\chi}\,\zeta\sqrt{P}\,(\hat{c}\chi R)^{l-1}(R_{\mathrm{mat}})^{\Psi-l}.
Proof.

Consider two encoders that differ only in their layer-ll parameter vectors, denoted by θ¯l\bar{\theta}_{l} and θ¯l′\bar{\theta}_{l}^{\prime}. By (7) and the 11-Lipschitz continuity of ReLU,

‖r¯l−r¯l′‖2\displaystyle\|\bar{r}_{l}-\bar{r}_{l}^{\prime}\|_{2} =‖ReLU⁡(𝐑¯l−1​θ¯l)−ReLU⁡(𝐑¯l−1​θ¯l′)‖2\displaystyle=\left\|\operatorname{ReLU}\left(\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{l-1}\bar{\theta}_{l}\right)-\operatorname{ReLU}\left(\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{l-1}\bar{\theta}_{l}^{\prime}\right)\right\|_{2}
≤‖𝐑¯l−1​(θ¯l−θ¯l′)‖2\displaystyle\leq\left\|\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{l-1}(\bar{\theta}_{l}-\bar{\theta}_{l}^{\prime})\right\|_{2}
≤‖𝐑¯l−1‖2​‖θ¯l−θ¯l′‖2.\displaystyle\leq\|\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{l-1}\|_{2}\|\bar{\theta}_{l}-\bar{\theta}_{l}^{\prime}\|_{2}. (41)

By Lemma 6, every entry of the input to layer ll is bounded in magnitude by

ζ​P​(c^​χ​R)l−1.\zeta\sqrt{P}(\hat{c}\chi R)^{l-1}.

Each block 𝐑^l−1\hat{\mathbf{R}}_{l-1} has TlT_{l} rows and c^​χ\hat{c}\chi entries per row. Since 𝐑¯l−1\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{l-1} is block diagonal with copies of 𝐑^l−1\hat{\mathbf{R}}_{l-1},

‖𝐑¯l−1‖2=‖𝐑^l−1‖2≤‖𝐑^l−1‖F.\|\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{l-1}\|_{2}=\|\hat{\mathbf{R}}_{l-1}\|_{2}\leq\|\hat{\mathbf{R}}_{l-1}\|_{F}.

Therefore,

‖𝐑¯l−1‖2\displaystyle\|\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{l-1}\|_{2} ≤Tl​c^​χ​ζ​P​(c^​χ​R)l−1\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{T_{l}\hat{c}\chi}\,\zeta\sqrt{P}(\hat{c}\chi R)^{l-1} (42)
‖r¯l−r¯l′‖2≤Tl​c^​χ​ζ​P​(c^​χ​R)l−1​‖θ¯l−θ¯l′‖2.\displaystyle\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\|\bar{r}_{l}-\bar{r}_{l}^{\prime}\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{T_{l}\hat{c}\chi}\zeta\sqrt{P}(\hat{c}\chi R)^{l-1}\|\bar{\theta}_{l}-\bar{\theta}_{l}^{\prime}\|_{2}. (43)

The perturbation then propagates through layers l+1,…,Ψl+1,\dots,\Psi. As in the proof of Lemma 1, each subsequent layer contributes at most its spectral norm. Thus,

‖f⁡(x,θ¯1,…,θ¯l,…,θ¯Ψ)−f⁡(x,θ¯1,…,θ¯l′,…,θ¯Ψ)‖2\displaystyle\|f(x;\bar{\theta}_{1},\dots,\bar{\theta}_{l},\dots,\bar{\theta}_{\Psi})-f(x;\bar{\theta}_{1},\dots,\bar{\theta}_{l}^{\prime},\dots,\bar{\theta}_{\Psi})\|_{2}
≤(∏j=l+1Ψ‖Θ¯j‖2)​Tl​c^​χ​ζ​P​(c^​χ​R)l−1​‖θ¯l−θ¯l′‖2\displaystyle\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\leq\left(\prod_{j=l+1}^{\Psi}\|\bar{\Theta}_{j}\|_{2}\right)\sqrt{T_{l}\hat{c}\chi}\zeta\sqrt{P}(\hat{c}\chi R)^{l-1}\|\bar{\theta}_{l}-\bar{\theta}_{l}^{\prime}\|_{2}
≤(Rmat)Ψ−l​Tl​c^​χ​ζ​P​(c^​χ​R)l−1​‖θ¯l−θ¯l′‖2.\displaystyle\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\leq(R_{\mathrm{mat}})^{\Psi-l}\sqrt{T_{l}\hat{c}\chi}\zeta\sqrt{P}(\hat{c}\chi R)^{l-1}\|\bar{\theta}_{l}-\bar{\theta}_{l}^{\prime}\|_{2}. (44)

Therefore, the encoder is Lθ​(l)L_{\theta}(l)-Lipschitz with respect to θ¯l\bar{\theta}_{l}. ∎

Lemma 3.

The encoder output is bounded elementwise by

ζ​P​(c^​χ​R)Ψ.\zeta\sqrt{P}\,(\hat{c}\chi R)^{\Psi}.
Proof.

By Lemma 6, every activation at layer ll is bounded in magnitude by

ζ​P​(c^​χ​R)l.\zeta\sqrt{P}\,(\hat{c}\chi R)^{l}.

Setting l=Ψl=\Psi gives the stated bound on the encoder output. ∎

Corollary 1.

Wherever it exists, the Jacobian of the encoder f⁡(x,θ¯1,…,θ¯Ψ)f(x;\bar{\theta}_{1},\dots,\bar{\theta}_{\Psi}) with respect to θ¯l\bar{\theta}_{l} has spectral norm bounded by Lθ​(l)L_{\theta}(l); that is,

‖Jθ¯l​(x)‖2≤Lθ​(l).\left\|J_{\bar{\theta}_{l}}(x)\right\|_{2}\leq L_{\theta}(l).
Proof.

Fix an input xx and a layer index ll, and define

g⁡(θ¯l)≜f⁡(x,θ¯1,…,θ¯l,…,θ¯Ψ),g(\bar{\theta}_{l})\triangleq f(x;\bar{\theta}_{1},\dots,\bar{\theta}_{l},\dots,\bar{\theta}_{\Psi}),

with all parameter blocks {θ¯j}j≠l\{\bar{\theta}_{j}\}_{j\neq l} held fixed. By Lemma 2, gg is Lθ​(l)L_{\theta}(l)-Lipschitz; hence, for all θ¯l\bar{\theta}_{l} and θ¯l′\bar{\theta}_{l}^{\prime},

‖g⁡(θ¯l)−g⁡(θ¯l′)‖2≤Lθ​(l)​‖θ¯l−θ¯l′‖2.\|g(\bar{\theta}_{l})-g(\bar{\theta}_{l}^{\prime})\|_{2}\leq L_{\theta}(l)\,\|\bar{\theta}_{l}-\bar{\theta}_{l}^{\prime}\|_{2}.

Assume that gg is differentiable at the point of interest. For any direction uu with ‖u‖2=1\|u\|_{2}=1 and any t≠0t\neq 0,

‖g⁡(θ¯l+t​u)−g⁡(θ¯l)‖2|t|≤Lθ​(l).\frac{\|g(\bar{\theta}_{l}+tu)-g(\bar{\theta}_{l})\|_{2}}{|t|}\leq L_{\theta}(l).

Taking the limit as t→0t\to 0 gives

‖Jθ¯l​(x)​u‖2≤Lθ​(l).\|J_{\bar{\theta}_{l}}(x)u\|_{2}\leq L_{\theta}(l).

Therefore,

‖Jθ¯l​(x)‖2=sup‖u‖2=1‖Jθ¯l​(x)​u‖2≤Lθ​(l).\|J_{\bar{\theta}_{l}}(x)\|_{2}=\sup_{\|u\|_{2}=1}\|J_{\bar{\theta}_{l}}(x)u\|_{2}\leq L_{\theta}(l).

∎

Corollary 2.

The gradients of the loss function with respect to the encoder outputs are bounded by some constant G>0G>0; that is,

‖∇zr​e​fℒ​(zr​e​f,zp​o​s,{zkn​e​g}k=1K)‖2\displaystyle\left\|\nabla_{z^{ref}}\mathcal{L}(z^{ref},z^{pos},\{z_{k}^{neg}\}_{k=1}^{K})\right\|_{2} ≤G,\displaystyle\leq G, (45)
‖∇zp​o​sℒ​(zr​e​f,zp​o​s,{zkn​e​g}k=1K)‖2\displaystyle\left\|\nabla_{z^{pos}}\mathcal{L}(z^{ref},z^{pos},\{z_{k}^{neg}\}_{k=1}^{K})\right\|_{2} ≤G,\displaystyle\leq G, (46)
‖∇zkn​e​gℒ​(zr​e​f,zp​o​s,{zkn​e​g}k=1K)‖2\displaystyle\left\|\nabla_{z_{k}^{neg}}\mathcal{L}(z^{ref},z^{pos},\{z_{k}^{neg}\}_{k=1}^{K})\right\|_{2} ≤G,k=1,…,K.\displaystyle\leq G,\qquad k=1,\dots,K. (47)
Proof.

Let Bz>0B_{z}>0 satisfy

‖zr​e​f‖2,‖zp​o​s‖2,‖zkn​e​g‖2≤Bz,k=1,…,K.\|z^{ref}\|_{2},\;\|z^{pos}\|_{2},\;\|z_{k}^{neg}\|_{2}\leq B_{z},\qquad k=1,\dots,K.

For the triplet loss

ℒ=−log⁡σ⁡((zr​e​f)T​zp​o​s)−∑k=1Klog⁡σ⁡(−(zr​e​f)T​zkn​e​g),\mathcal{L}=-\log\sigma\big((z^{ref})^{T}z^{pos}\big)-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\log\sigma\big(-(z^{ref})^{T}z_{k}^{neg}\big),

the gradients are

∇zr​e​fℒ\displaystyle\nabla_{z^{ref}}\mathcal{L} =−[1−σ⁡((zr​e​f)T​zp​o​s)]​zp​o​s+∑k=1Kσ⁡((zr​e​f)T​zkn​e​g)​zkn​e​g,\displaystyle=-\left[1-\sigma\big((z^{ref})^{T}z^{pos}\big)\right]z^{pos}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sigma\big((z^{ref})^{T}z_{k}^{neg}\big)z_{k}^{neg}, (48)
∇zp​o​sℒ\displaystyle\nabla_{z^{pos}}\mathcal{L} =−[1−σ⁡((zr​e​f)T​zp​o​s)]​zr​e​f,\displaystyle=-\left[1-\sigma\big((z^{ref})^{T}z^{pos}\big)\right]z^{ref}, (49)
∇zkn​e​gℒ\displaystyle\nabla_{z_{k}^{neg}}\mathcal{L} =σ⁡((zr​e​f)T​zkn​e​g)​zr​e​f.\displaystyle=\sigma\big((z^{ref})^{T}z_{k}^{neg}\big)z^{ref}. (50)

Since 0≤σ⁡(a)≤10\leq\sigma(a)\leq 1 for all a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R},

‖∇zr​e​fℒ‖2\displaystyle\|\nabla_{z^{ref}}\mathcal{L}\|_{2} ≤‖zp​o​s‖2+∑k=1K‖zkn​e​g‖2≤(K+1)​Bz,\displaystyle\leq\|z^{pos}\|_{2}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\|z_{k}^{neg}\|_{2}\leq(K+1)B_{z}, (51)
‖∇zp​o​sℒ‖2\displaystyle\|\nabla_{z^{pos}}\mathcal{L}\|_{2} ≤‖zr​e​f‖2≤Bz,\displaystyle\leq\|z^{ref}\|_{2}\leq B_{z}, (52)
‖∇zkn​e​gℒ‖2\displaystyle\|\nabla_{z_{k}^{neg}}\mathcal{L}\|_{2} ≤‖zr​e​f‖2≤Bz.\displaystyle\leq\|z^{ref}\|_{2}\leq B_{z}. (53)

G=(K+1)​Bz.G=(K+1)B_{z}.

A-A3 Proof of Lemma 4

Lemma 4.

The triplet loss function ℒ⁡(zr​e​f,zp​o​s,{zkn​e​g}k=1K)\mathcal{L}(z^{ref},z^{pos},\{z_{k}^{neg}\}_{k=1}^{K}) is Γ\Gamma-smooth with respect to the concatenated vector [zr​e​f,zp​o​s,z1n​e​g,…,zKn​e​g][z^{ref},z^{pos},z_{1}^{neg},\dots,z_{K}^{neg}], where Γ=K+2​max⁡{Γr​e​f,Γp​n}\Gamma=\sqrt{K+2}\max\{\Gamma_{ref},\Gamma_{pn}\} and

Γr​e​f\displaystyle\Gamma_{ref} =2​(TΨ​ζ)2​P​(c^​χ​R)2​Ψ​K2\displaystyle=2(T_{\Psi}\zeta)^{2}P(\hat{c}\chi R)^{2\Psi}K^{2}
+(4​(TΨ​ζ)2​P​(c^​χ​R)2​Ψ+1)​K\displaystyle\quad+\left(4(T_{\Psi}\zeta)^{2}P(\hat{c}\chi R)^{2\Psi}+1\right)K
+2​(TΨ​ζ)2​P​(c^​χ​R)2​Ψ+1,\displaystyle\quad+2(T_{\Psi}\zeta)^{2}P(\hat{c}\chi R)^{2\Psi}+1, (54)
Γp​n\displaystyle\Gamma_{pn} =2​(K+1)​(TΨ​ζ)2​P​(c^​χ​R)2​Ψ+1.\displaystyle=2(K+1)(T_{\Psi}\zeta)^{2}P(\hat{c}\chi R)^{2\Psi}+1. (55)
Proof.

We prove that the triplet loss is smooth with respect to the encoder outputs associated with the reference, positive, and negative signals. Define

gloss​(z~+,{z~k−}k=1K)\displaystyle g_{\mathrm{loss}}\left(\tilde{z}^{+},\{\tilde{z}_{k}^{-}\}_{k=1}^{K}\right) =−log⁡(σ⁡(z~+))−∑k=1Klog⁡(σ⁡(−z~k−)).\displaystyle=-\log\left(\sigma(\tilde{z}^{+})\right)-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\log\left(\sigma(-\tilde{z}_{k}^{-})\right). (56)

Each term of glossg_{\mathrm{loss}} is a scalar logistic loss whose second derivative is bounded by 1/41/4. Hence, the Hessian of glossg_{\mathrm{loss}} is diagonal with spectral norm at most 1/41/4. In particular, glossg_{\mathrm{loss}} is 11-smooth with respect to z~+,z~1−,…,z~K−\tilde{z}^{+},\tilde{z}_{1}^{-},\dots,\tilde{z}_{K}^{-}.

The triplet loss can be written as

ℒ⁡(zr​e​f,zp​o​s,{zkn​e​g}k=1K)=gloss​((zr​e​f)T​zp​o​s,{(zr​e​f)T​zkn​e​g}k=1K).\mathcal{L}\left(z^{ref},z^{pos},\{z_{k}^{neg}\}_{k=1}^{K}\right)=g_{\mathrm{loss}}\left((z^{ref})^{T}z^{pos},\{(z^{ref})^{T}z_{k}^{neg}\}_{k=1}^{K}\right).

Its smoothness with respect to the encoder outputs requires these outputs to be bounded. By Lemma 3, every encoder output is elementwise bounded by ζ​P​(c^​χ​R)Ψ\zeta\sqrt{P}(\hat{c}\chi R)^{\Psi}. Since the encoder output contains TΨT_{\Psi} entries,

‖z‖2≤TΨ​ζ​P​(c^​χ​R)Ψ≤TΨ​ζ​P​(c^​χ​R)Ψ.\|z\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{T_{\Psi}}\,\zeta\sqrt{P}(\hat{c}\chi R)^{\Psi}\leq T_{\Psi}\zeta\sqrt{P}(\hat{c}\chi R)^{\Psi}.

For notational convenience, define

Benc=TΨ​ζ​P​(c^​χ​R)Ψ.B_{\mathrm{enc}}=T_{\Psi}\zeta\sqrt{P}(\hat{c}\chi R)^{\Psi}.

The gradient of the loss with respect to the concatenated encoder outputs is

∇ℒ​(zr​e​f,zp​o​s,{zkn​e​g}k=1K)\displaystyle\nabla\mathcal{L}\left(z^{ref},z^{pos},\{z_{k}^{neg}\}_{k=1}^{K}\right)
=[zp​o​s​∇z~+gloss+∑k=1Kzkn​e​g​∇z~k−glosszr​e​f​∇z~+glosszr​e​f​∇z~1−glosszr​e​f​∇z~K−gloss],\displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}z^{pos}\nabla_{\tilde{z}^{+}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}+\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}z_{k}^{neg}\nabla_{\tilde{z}_{k}^{-}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}\\[5.69054pt] z^{ref}\nabla_{\tilde{z}^{+}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}\\ z^{ref}\nabla_{\tilde{z}_{1}^{-}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}\\ \vdots\\ z^{ref}\nabla_{\tilde{z}_{K}^{-}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}\end{bmatrix}, (57)

where all derivatives of glossg_{\mathrm{loss}} are evaluated at

((zr​e​f)T​zp​o​s,{(zr​e​f)T​zkn​e​g}k=1K).\left((z^{ref})^{T}z^{pos},\{(z^{ref})^{T}z_{k}^{neg}\}_{k=1}^{K}\right).

Consider another collection of encoder outputs zr​e​f′z^{ref^{\prime}}, zp​o​s′z^{pos^{\prime}}, and {zkn​e​g′}k=1K\{z_{k}^{neg^{\prime}}\}_{k=1}^{K}. By the triangle inequality,

‖∇ℒ​(zr​e​f,zp​o​s,{zkn​e​g}k=1K)−∇ℒ​(zr​e​f′,zp​o​s′,{zkn​e​g′}k=1K)‖2\displaystyle\left\|\nabla\mathcal{L}\left(z^{ref},z^{pos},\{z_{k}^{neg}\}_{k=1}^{K}\right)-\nabla\mathcal{L}\left(z^{ref^{\prime}},z^{pos^{\prime}},\{z_{k}^{neg^{\prime}}\}_{k=1}^{K}\right)\right\|_{2}
≤‖zp​o​s​∇z~+gloss−zp​o​s′​∇z~+gloss′‖2\displaystyle\leq\left\|z^{pos}\nabla_{\tilde{z}^{+}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}-z^{pos^{\prime}}\nabla_{\tilde{z}^{+}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\prime}\right\|_{2}
+∑k=1K‖zkn​e​g∇z~k−gloss−zkn​e​g′∇z~k−gloss′‖2\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left\|z_{k}^{neg}\nabla_{\tilde{z}_{k}^{-}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}-z_{k}^{neg^{\prime}}\nabla_{\tilde{z}_{k}^{-}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\prime}\right\|_{2}
+‖zr​e​f​∇z~+gloss−zr​e​f′​∇z~+gloss′‖2\displaystyle\quad+\left\|z^{ref}\nabla_{\tilde{z}^{+}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}-z^{ref^{\prime}}\nabla_{\tilde{z}^{+}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\prime}\right\|_{2}
+∑k=1K‖zr​e​f∇z~k−gloss−zr​e​f′∇z~k−gloss′‖2,\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left\|z^{ref}\nabla_{\tilde{z}_{k}^{-}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}-z^{ref^{\prime}}\nabla_{\tilde{z}_{k}^{-}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\prime}\right\|_{2}, (58)

where the unprimed derivatives are evaluated at

((zr​e​f)T​zp​o​s,{(zr​e​f)T​zkn​e​g}k=1K),\left((z^{ref})^{T}z^{pos},\{(z^{ref})^{T}z_{k}^{neg}\}_{k=1}^{K}\right),

and the primed derivatives are evaluated at

((zr​e​f′)T​zp​o​s′,{(zr​e​f′)T​zkn​e​g′}k=1K).\left((z^{ref^{\prime}})^{T}z^{pos^{\prime}},\{(z^{ref^{\prime}})^{T}z_{k}^{neg^{\prime}}\}_{k=1}^{K}\right).

For the first term, add and subtract zp​o​s′​∇z~+glossz^{pos^{\prime}}\nabla_{\tilde{z}^{+}}g_{\mathrm{loss}} to obtain

‖zp​o​s​∇z~+gloss−zp​o​s′​∇z~+gloss′‖2\displaystyle\left\|z^{pos}\nabla_{\tilde{z}^{+}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}-z^{pos^{\prime}}\nabla_{\tilde{z}^{+}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\prime}\right\|_{2}
≤‖zp​o​s−zp​o​s′‖2​‖∇z~+gloss‖2\displaystyle\leq\|z^{pos}-z^{pos^{\prime}}\|_{2}\left\|\nabla_{\tilde{z}^{+}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}\right\|_{2}
+‖zp​o​s′‖2​‖∇z~+gloss−∇z~+gloss′‖2\displaystyle\quad+\|z^{pos^{\prime}}\|_{2}\left\|\nabla_{\tilde{z}^{+}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}-\nabla_{\tilde{z}^{+}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\prime}\right\|_{2}

Similarly,

∑k=1K‖zkn​e​g​∇z~k−gloss−zkn​e​g′​∇z~k−gloss′‖2\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left\|z_{k}^{neg}\nabla_{\tilde{z}_{k}^{-}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}-z_{k}^{neg^{\prime}}\nabla_{\tilde{z}_{k}^{-}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\prime}\right\|_{2}

and

‖zr​e​f​∇z~+gloss−zr​e​f′​∇z~+gloss′‖2\displaystyle\left\|z^{ref}\nabla_{\tilde{z}^{+}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}-z^{ref^{\prime}}\nabla_{\tilde{z}^{+}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\prime}\right\|_{2}

∑k=1K‖zr​e​f​∇z~k−gloss−zr​e​f′​∇z~k−gloss′‖2\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left\|z^{ref}\nabla_{\tilde{z}_{k}^{-}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}-z^{ref^{\prime}}\nabla_{\tilde{z}_{k}^{-}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\prime}\right\|_{2}

‖∇z~k−gloss−∇z~k−gloss′‖2\displaystyle\left\|\nabla_{\tilde{z}_{k}^{-}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}-\nabla_{\tilde{z}_{k}^{-}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\prime}\right\|_{2}

+∑j=1K|(zr​e​f)Tzjn​e​g−(zr​e​f′)Tzjn​e​g′|.\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{j=1}^{K}\left|(z^{ref})^{T}z_{j}^{neg}-(z^{ref^{\prime}})^{T}z_{j}^{neg^{\prime}}\right|. (63)

For the positive-pair inner product,

≤‖zp​o​s‖2​‖zr​e​f−zr​e​f′‖2+‖zr​e​f′‖2​‖zp​o​s−zp​o​s′‖2\displaystyle\leq\|z^{pos}\|_{2}\|z^{ref}-z^{ref^{\prime}}\|_{2}+\|z^{ref^{\prime}}\|_{2}\|z^{pos}-z^{pos^{\prime}}\|_{2}
≤Benc​‖zr​e​f−zr​e​f′‖2+Benc​‖zp​o​s−zp​o​s′‖2.\displaystyle\leq B_{\mathrm{enc}}\|z^{ref}-z^{ref^{\prime}}\|_{2}+B_{\mathrm{enc}}\|z^{pos}-z^{pos^{\prime}}\|_{2}. (65)

Likewise, for each negative sample,

|(zr​e​f)T​zkn​e​g−(zr​e​f′)T​zkn​e​g′|\displaystyle\left|(z^{ref})^{T}z_{k}^{neg}-(z^{ref^{\prime}})^{T}z_{k}^{neg^{\prime}}\right|

‖∇z~k−gloss−∇z~k−gloss′‖2\displaystyle\left\|\nabla_{\tilde{z}_{k}^{-}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}-\nabla_{\tilde{z}_{k}^{-}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\prime}\right\|_{2}
≤Benc​(K+1)​‖zr​e​f−zr​e​f′‖2+Benc​‖zp​o​s−zp​o​s′‖2\displaystyle\leq B_{\mathrm{enc}}(K+1)\|z^{ref}-z^{ref^{\prime}}\|_{2}+B_{\mathrm{enc}}\|z^{pos}-z^{pos^{\prime}}\|_{2}
+Benc∑j=1K∥zjn​e​g−zjn​e​g′∥2.\displaystyle\quad+B_{\mathrm{enc}}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\|z_{j}^{neg}-z_{j}^{neg^{\prime}}\|_{2}. (67)

The same bound holds for ‖∇z~+gloss−∇z~+gloss′‖2\|\nabla_{\tilde{z}^{+}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}-\nabla_{\tilde{z}^{+}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\prime}\|_{2}.

Substituting these bounds into the preceding inequalities gives

‖zp​o​s​∇z~+gloss−zp​o​s′​∇z~+gloss′‖2\displaystyle\left\|z^{pos}\nabla_{\tilde{z}^{+}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}-z^{pos^{\prime}}\nabla_{\tilde{z}^{+}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\prime}\right\|_{2}
≤Benc2​(K+1)​‖zr​e​f−zr​e​f′‖2\displaystyle\leq B_{\mathrm{enc}}^{2}(K+1)\|z^{ref}-z^{ref^{\prime}}\|_{2}
+(Benc2+1)​‖zp​o​s−zp​o​s′‖2\displaystyle\quad+(B_{\mathrm{enc}}^{2}+1)\|z^{pos}-z^{pos^{\prime}}\|_{2}
+Benc2∑k=1K∥zkn​e​g−zkn​e​g′∥2,\displaystyle\quad+B_{\mathrm{enc}}^{2}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\|z_{k}^{neg}-z_{k}^{neg^{\prime}}\|_{2}, (68)
∑k=1K‖zkn​e​g​∇z~k−gloss−zkn​e​g′​∇z~k−gloss′‖2\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left\|z_{k}^{neg}\nabla_{\tilde{z}_{k}^{-}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}-z_{k}^{neg^{\prime}}\nabla_{\tilde{z}_{k}^{-}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\prime}\right\|_{2}
≤K⁡(K+1)​Benc2​‖zr​e​f−zr​e​f′‖2\displaystyle\leq K(K+1)B_{\mathrm{enc}}^{2}\|z^{ref}-z^{ref^{\prime}}\|_{2}
+K​Benc2​‖zp​o​s−zp​o​s′‖2\displaystyle\quad+KB_{\mathrm{enc}}^{2}\|z^{pos}-z^{pos^{\prime}}\|_{2}
+(KBenc2+1)∑k=1K∥zkn​e​g−zkn​e​g′∥2,\displaystyle\quad+(KB_{\mathrm{enc}}^{2}+1)\sum_{k=1}^{K}\|z_{k}^{neg}-z_{k}^{neg^{\prime}}\|_{2}, (69)
‖zr​e​f​∇z~+gloss−zr​e​f′​∇z~+gloss′‖2\displaystyle\left\|z^{ref}\nabla_{\tilde{z}^{+}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}-z^{ref^{\prime}}\nabla_{\tilde{z}^{+}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\prime}\right\|_{2}
≤(Benc2​K+Benc2+1)​‖zr​e​f−zr​e​f′‖2\displaystyle\leq(B_{\mathrm{enc}}^{2}K+B_{\mathrm{enc}}^{2}+1)\|z^{ref}-z^{ref^{\prime}}\|_{2}
+Benc2​‖zp​o​s−zp​o​s′‖2\displaystyle\quad+B_{\mathrm{enc}}^{2}\|z^{pos}-z^{pos^{\prime}}\|_{2}

and

∑k=1K‖zr​e​f​∇z~k−gloss−zr​e​f′​∇z~k−gloss′‖2\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left\|z^{ref}\nabla_{\tilde{z}_{k}^{-}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}-z^{ref^{\prime}}\nabla_{\tilde{z}_{k}^{-}}g_{\mathrm{loss}}^{\prime}\right\|_{2} ≤K⁡(Benc2​K+Benc2+1)​‖zr​e​f−zr​e​f′‖2+K​Benc2​‖zp​o​s−zp​o​s′‖2\displaystyle\leq K(B_{\mathrm{enc}}^{2}K+B_{\mathrm{enc}}^{2}+1)\|z^{ref}-z^{ref^{\prime}}\|_{2}+KB_{\mathrm{enc}}^{2}\|z^{pos}-z^{pos^{\prime}}\|_{2}
+KBenc2∑k=1K∥zkn​e​g−zkn​e​g′∥2.\displaystyle+KB_{\mathrm{enc}}^{2}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\|z_{k}^{neg}-z_{k}^{neg^{\prime}}\|_{2}. (71)

≤[2​Benc2​K2+(4​Benc2+1)​K+2​Benc2+1]​‖zr​e​f−zr​e​f′‖2\displaystyle\leq\left[2B_{\mathrm{enc}}^{2}K^{2}+(4B_{\mathrm{enc}}^{2}+1)K+2B_{\mathrm{enc}}^{2}+1\right]\|z^{ref}-z^{ref^{\prime}}\|_{2}
+[2​(K+1)​Benc2+1]​‖zp​o​s−zp​o​s′‖2\displaystyle\quad+\left[2(K+1)B_{\mathrm{enc}}^{2}+1\right]\|z^{pos}-z^{pos^{\prime}}\|_{2}
+[2(K+1)Benc2+1]∑k=1K∥zkn​e​g−zkn​e​g′∥2.\displaystyle\quad+\left[2(K+1)B_{\mathrm{enc}}^{2}+1\right]\sum_{k=1}^{K}\|z_{k}^{neg}-z_{k}^{neg^{\prime}}\|_{2}. (72)

Substituting Benc=TΨ​ζ​P​(c^​χ​R)ΨB_{\mathrm{enc}}=T_{\Psi}\zeta\sqrt{P}(\hat{c}\chi R)^{\Psi} gives

Γr​e​f\displaystyle\Gamma_{ref} =2​(TΨ​ζ)2​P​(c^​χ​R)2​Ψ​K2\displaystyle=2(T_{\Psi}\zeta)^{2}P(\hat{c}\chi R)^{2\Psi}K^{2}
+(4​(TΨ​ζ)2​P​(c^​χ​R)2​Ψ+1)​K\displaystyle\quad+\left(4(T_{\Psi}\zeta)^{2}P(\hat{c}\chi R)^{2\Psi}+1\right)K
+2​(TΨ​ζ)2​P​(c^​χ​R)2​Ψ+1,\displaystyle\quad+2(T_{\Psi}\zeta)^{2}P(\hat{c}\chi R)^{2\Psi}+1, (73)
Γp​n\displaystyle\Gamma_{pn} =2​(K+1)​(TΨ​ζ)2​P​(c^​χ​R)2​Ψ+1.\displaystyle=2(K+1)(T_{\Psi}\zeta)^{2}P(\hat{c}\chi R)^{2\Psi}+1. (74)

Let

Γ~=max⁡{Γr​e​f,Γp​n}.\widetilde{\Gamma}=\max\{\Gamma_{ref},\Gamma_{pn}\}.

Then

‖∇ℒ​(zr​e​f,zp​o​s,{zkn​e​g}k=1K)−∇ℒ​(zr​e​f′,zp​o​s′,{zkn​e​g′}k=1K)‖2\displaystyle\left\|\nabla\mathcal{L}\left(z^{ref},z^{pos},\{z_{k}^{neg}\}_{k=1}^{K}\right)-\nabla\mathcal{L}\left(z^{ref^{\prime}},z^{pos^{\prime}},\{z_{k}^{neg^{\prime}}\}_{k=1}^{K}\right)\right\|_{2}
≤Γ~​(‖zr​e​f−zr​e​f′‖2+‖zp​o​s−zp​o​s′‖2+∑k=1K‖zkn​e​g−zkn​e​g′‖2).\displaystyle\leq\widetilde{\Gamma}\left(\|z^{ref}-z^{ref^{\prime}}\|_{2}+\|z^{pos}-z^{pos^{\prime}}\|_{2}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\|z_{k}^{neg}-z_{k}^{neg^{\prime}}\|_{2}\right). (75)

Define

zstacked=[zr​e​fzp​o​sz1n​e​gzKn​e​g],zstacked′=[zr​e​f′zp​o​s′z1n​e​g′zKn​e​g′].z_{\mathrm{stacked}}=\begin{bmatrix}z^{ref}\\ z^{pos}\\ z_{1}^{neg}\\ \vdots\\ z_{K}^{neg}\end{bmatrix},\qquad z_{\mathrm{stacked}}^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}z^{ref^{\prime}}\\ z^{pos^{\prime}}\\ z_{1}^{neg^{\prime}}\\ \vdots\\ z_{K}^{neg^{\prime}}\end{bmatrix}.

By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,

‖zr​e​f−zr​e​f′‖2+‖zp​o​s−zp​o​s′‖2+∑k=1K‖zkn​e​g−zkn​e​g′‖2\displaystyle\|z^{ref}-z^{ref^{\prime}}\|_{2}+\|z^{pos}-z^{pos^{\prime}}\|_{2}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\|z_{k}^{neg}-z_{k}^{neg^{\prime}}\|_{2}
≤K+2​‖zstacked−zstacked′‖2.\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{K+2}\,\|z_{\mathrm{stacked}}-z_{\mathrm{stacked}}^{\prime}\|_{2}. (76)

Therefore,

‖∇ℒ​(zstacked)−∇ℒ​(zstacked′)‖2\displaystyle\left\|\nabla\mathcal{L}(z_{\mathrm{stacked}})-\nabla\mathcal{L}(z_{\mathrm{stacked}}^{\prime})\right\|_{2}
≤K+2​Γ~​‖zstacked−zstacked′‖2.\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{K+2}\,\widetilde{\Gamma}\,\|z_{\mathrm{stacked}}-z_{\mathrm{stacked}}^{\prime}\|_{2}. (77)

Thus, the triplet loss is Γ\Gamma-smooth with

Γ=K+2​max⁡{Γr​e​f,Γp​n}.\Gamma=\sqrt{K+2}\max\{\Gamma_{ref},\Gamma_{pn}\}.
